# Addendum — the semantic map + health surface (`ptl-backtesting`)

**Why this file exists:** the `ref:ptl-backtesting` researcher was scoped to the Next.js app and the two
static HTML documents and therefore missed this surface entirely. The user called it out by name. This
addendum covers it. **Form only — see BRIEF §3a and §3b-bis. Every string, number and subject in the
source file is forbidden material; nothing below reproduces any of it.**

Source: `apps/live_trades_dashboard.py` (Streamlit + Plotly, 2910 lines).
Relevant functions: `_semantic_coords:879`, `_render_semantic_map:896`, `_render_semantic_map_all:2571`,
`_render_onchain_health:1504`, `_render_sync_freshness:1494`.

---

## 1. The map of all the links — how it is actually drawn

Each item is a *question*. The question text is embedded (`sentence-transformers all-MiniLM-L6-v2`),
the embeddings are projected to 2D with **UMAP**, and the result is drawn as a marker-only scatter.
The cross-batch variant pools everything into **one** UMAP fit so clusters stay comparable
(`_render_semantic_map_all:2571`).

The rendering decisions are the interesting part:

| Decision | Value | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Axes | `visible=False`, `showgrid=False`, `zeroline=False` on **both** | **The space has no coordinates.** There is nothing to read off. Position means only "near these other questions". |
| Backgrounds | `paper_bgcolor` and `plot_bgcolor` both `rgba(0,0,0,0)` | The plot has no surface of its own — it floats directly on the page ground and inherits the theme. |
| Margins | `t:10 b:10 l:0 r:0` | No framing, no padding, no chrome. The field bleeds to the container edge. |
| Marker size | `max(8, sqrt(magnitude) * 3.5)`, `sizemode="diameter"` | Square-root scaling — magnitude is felt, not measured. |
| Marker outline | `0.5px rgba(255,255,255,0.25)` | A hairline that separates overlapping points without competing with fill. Same 1px-hairline instinct as everywhere else in PTL. |
| Colour | diverging, symmetric via `cmid=0`, on a **signed-log** scale | Both directions from a true centre. |
| Height | fixed 600 | |
| Caption | one plain sentence naming every encoding | The house "hard thing, then an honest gloss" move again. |

**The transferable idea:** *a field of questions positioned by meaning, on an invisible coordinate
system, floating on the page ground with no frame.* Proximity is the only channel. That is a
scroll-world-ready visual that is native to how PTL actually thinks, and it illustrates *uncertainty
being organised* rather than anything about markets.

⚠️ **Colour is the one thing that must NOT transfer.** Here the diverging red→green ramp encodes
outcome magnitude. On the landing page any diverging red/green ramp over a field of points reads as
profit and loss to exactly the audience we are hiding it from. The landing page's field must be
**monochrome**, or encode something with no valence at all (e.g. depth/recency). See §3.

## 2. The health surface — and the best non-leaking idea in the whole study

`_render_onchain_health` and its neighbours exist to **fail loud**. The rules, in the code's own terms:

- A view whose underlying data is not trustworthy gets *"an unmissable banner"* (`:1507`).
- Three graded tiers: hard error (data untrustworthy), warning (present but not authoritative),
  warning (present, authoritative, but stale beyond a threshold).
- Every message states **what is wrong, why it matters, and the exact remedy** — a named button or a
  literal command to run. No apology, no "something went wrong".
- Thresholds carry their reasoning inline: the staleness banner fires at 3h because *"the hourly cron
  has missed two cycles"*; below that a thing is *"simply between sweeps, which is not staleness worth
  a banner"* (`:1526-1528`).
- Freshness renders as a single caption line of chips joined by `·`.
- A subtle one: the check reads *last-swept*, not last-activity, because *"a wallet that has stopped
  trading is still healthy"* (`:1498`) — the system is careful not to confuse *idle* with *broken*.

And the line that matters most, from `_render_mtm_section:1554`:

> **"Nothing is rendered rather than showing estimates."**

When the pipeline cannot stand behind a number, the product **draws nothing at all**.

### Why this is the find

This is PTL's epistemic character stated in code, and — critically — **it is entirely sayable**. It is
about how a system treats its own uncertainty. It names no instrument, no venue, no product, and no
performance. It is the same spine as the brief's accountability argument, arriving from a completely
different direction: a machine that refuses to assert what it cannot back.

It also solves a real design problem. The page must *withhold* almost everything, and withholding
normally reads as evasive. But if restraint is presented as the company's **standard** rather than its
**secrecy** — we show you nothing we cannot stand behind — then the page's opacity becomes a
demonstration of the very principle it is describing. The mystery stops being a marketing device and
starts being the argument.

Pair this with `ptl-chat-py`'s **em-dash for absent data** (§7d of that report): PTL already has a
house glyph meaning *"this is deliberately not shown"*. Used sparingly, that is a mysterious and
completely honest device.

## 3. Composite: what the landing visual should inherit

Three PTL surfaces independently draw the same kind of object, and together they specify it:

| Source | Contribution |
|---|---|
| `ptl-backtesting` semantic map | A field of nodes positioned by **meaning**, axes invisible, transparent ground, hairline outlines, √-scaled sizes. |
| `ptl-trade` thesis map | Edges are **orthogonal right-angled pipework with 10px fillets** (hand-rolled lane router — *not* dagre, *not* bezier, *not* force-directed). **Edge opacity IS the information**: 0.15 resting, 0.04 dimmed, 0.7 focused, all in `currentColor`. The graph sits as a ghost; illumination selects one causal chain through the fog. |
| `ptl-chat-py` AST diagram | Top-down tree, straight edges, **no arrowheads**, node fill and node outline carrying two orthogonal encodings. |

**Therefore the landing visual, stated precisely:** a ghost field of linked questions, drawn in one ink
on the page ground with no frame and no axes, where **scroll illuminates a single chain through the
fog**. Nodes never move — PTL's house motion rule is that motion animates *state, never geometry*
(`ptl-trade`: nodes carry only `transition-opacity`; charts set `isAnimationActive={false}`; the sole
ambient animation in the product is a 1.5s opacity breath meaning "live").

This is a genuine scroll-world — a camera moving through a continuous world — but the camera moves
through **an argument** rather than a diorama, and it moves by *illumination* rather than translation.

Three things it buys us for free:
1. **It cannot leak.** A monochrome field of unlabelled nodes shows no instrument, no venue, no number.
2. **It is honest to the brief.** The problem is uncertainty and how events cascade; this draws exactly
   that and nothing more.
3. **Reduced-motion and performance fall out naturally.** Opacity-only animation with static geometry
   is cheap to render, and the reduced-motion fallback is simply the fully-lit graph — a legible
   static image, not a degraded one.

## 4. Rules this addendum adds to the build

1. No diverging red/green ramp anywhere on the page. Monochrome, or a single valence-free hue.
2. Nodes and edges carry **no labels that name anything real**. If nodes need text, it must be drawn
   from the allowed problem/approach vocabulary in BRIEF §3b, or nothing at all.
3. Motion animates opacity only. Geometry is static. Reduced-motion renders the lit state.
4. Edges are orthogonal with small fillets, in `currentColor`, at PTL's opacity ladder. No beziers, no
   force-directed jitter, no arrowheads.
5. If a value cannot be shown honestly, show an em-dash — and never invent a number to fill a slot.

Design phase is running: 1 spec → 4 independent directions → 2 adversarial judges each → 1 decision. 14 agents, all Opus 5 at max effort, halting on any failure.

**On the page you pointed me to — it was the most valuable reference in the study, and not for the reason I expected.**

The visual construction (`_render_semantic_map`, `live_trades_dashboard.py:896`) is exactly the right grammar for a landing visual. Every question gets embedded and UMAP-projected to 2D, then drawn as markers with:

- **both axes fully invisible** — the space has no coordinates, so position means only *"near these other questions"*
- **transparent paper and plot background** — the field floats directly on the page ground, no surface of its own
- **zero framing margins**, hairline `0.5px` marker outlines, √-scaled sizes

Combined with `ptl-trade`'s thesis map — which turned out **not** to be dagre-based at all, but a hand-rolled lane-graph router drawing orthogonal right-angled edges with 10px fillets, where **edge opacity *is* the information** (0.15 resting, 0.04 dimmed, 0.7 focused) — you get a native PTL scroll-world: *a ghost field of linked questions where scroll illuminates one chain through the fog.* The camera moves through an argument rather than a space, by illumination rather than translation. Nodes never move, which is PTL's actual house rule (motion animates state, never geometry) and makes reduced-motion trivial: the fallback is simply the fully-lit graph.

**But the better find was a sentence, not a visual.** From `_render_mtm_section:1554`, describing what happens when the data can't be trusted:

> *"Nothing is rendered rather than showing estimates."*

That is PTL's epistemic character stated in code — and it's completely sayable. It names no instrument, no venue, no product, no number. It's the brief's accountability argument arriving from another direction: *a machine that refuses to assert what it cannot back.*

It also solves the central design problem. This page has to withhold nearly everything, and withholding normally reads as evasive. But if restraint is framed as the company's **standard** rather than its **secrecy**, the page's opacity becomes a demonstration of the very principle it's describing. The mystery stops being a marketing device and becomes the argument. One of the four directions is built entirely on this.

Two hazards I've written into the brief as hard rules:

- **The colour encoding must not transfer.** In the source, the field is coloured by a diverging red→green ramp encoding outcome. On a public page, a red/green diverging ramp over a field of points reads as profit and loss to precisely the audience we're hiding it from. The landing field ships monochrome.
- **The instrument chrome invites numbers.** The metric-strip pattern (uppercase micro-label above a value) is beautiful and very PTL — but any number in that slot reads as performance, *including an invented placeholder*. So the page ships no metrics at all; the em-dash convention covers the gap, and it's honest rather than coy.

I'll report when the winner lands.

## 2b. THE STORY IS THE DESIGN — this overrides any competing emphasis

**The strength of this page is the copy.** Not the visual, not the chrome, not the scroll mechanic. The
argument carries the page; everything else exists to make someone keep reading it. If a design decision
and a sentence compete, the sentence wins.

### The arc — four beats, in this order

1. **This is the future.** Machines will make the consequential decisions — in finance, in business, in
   government. State it as a fact about the world, not as a prediction about us. The reader should feel
   the inevitability before they feel any pitch.
2. **This is how the future gets closer.** Not "here is our product" — the *condition* that has to be
   met for that future to arrive at all. Today's models summarise the written past; they do not forecast.
   The future is waiting on something that does not exist yet.
3. **This is the only way to solve it.** The heart. Accuracy alone cannot get there, because nothing in a
   benchmark makes a machine answerable — a confident error vanishes inside a good average, and software
   charges the same fee whether it was right or wrong. The only thing that produces judgment is
   **consequence**: a machine that commits something scarce, is answerable for being wrong, and improves
   when reality resolves. Make this feel like a discovered necessity, not a claim.
4. **How we do it — withheld.** The mechanism is where the page goes quiet. Not evasive, not coy:
   *deliberate*. The reader should finish convinced the problem is real, convinced there is only one way
   through it, and genuinely unable to say what PTL builds.

The reader's closing thought should be **"they're right, and I want to know how"** — never
*"what do they actually do?"* as a complaint. Curiosity, not confusion.

### Vagueness is directional, not uniform

Be sharp and concrete about the **problem** and about **why consequence is the only answer**. Be vague
only about **implementation** — what we build, what it runs on, what it touches, what it produces.
A reader should be able to argue the thesis back to a colleague and still not know the company's business.

### Concision is a hard requirement

**As short as it can be while still landing.** This is the discipline that makes the argument feel
inevitable rather than pleaded. Prefer a sentence to a paragraph, and a clause to a sentence. Cut every
line that merely restates a previous one — the current page has several. If a beat can be carried in six
words, it does not get twenty. Ruthlessness here is the difference between austere and windy.

### What the scroll is for

The scroll exists to **keep someone reading** — it is a pacing device for an argument, not a ride.
Each beat should earn the next scroll: the reader moves because they want the next line, not because
there is more page. Reveal on scroll should feel like the argument advancing. Never let the visual
outshine, delay, or talk over the sentence it accompanies; if a reader remembers the animation and not
the argument, the page has failed.

Predictive

Text Labs.

ptl.inc

Within a generation, machines will make most of the decisions that matter. Almost nothing about how we build them establishes which one has earned the right.

What we have

A language model is a memory. Superb at everything already written. Ask it what happens next and it answers, fluently, with the past.

Trained on
the written past
Answers with
the written past
Answers for
nothing—

An em dash is not a zero. It marks a place where nothing exists to report.

Temporal reasoning

Reasoning about what follows from what, and how long it takes.

Seeing how one event pulls the next, why a pattern repeats, which signals are doing the work. Not one more capability on the list: the primitive that separates a search engine from a partner in deciding.

The missing test

Suppose you had it. How would you know it was any good?

A benchmark will not tell you. It reports an average, and an average is where a confident, catastrophic error hides.

Software will not tell you either. Nothing happens to a model that was confidently wrong, and nothing happens to the people who built it.

Confidence is easy. Accountability is the part nobody builds.

Earning the right

Accountability cannot be measured afterwards. It has to be built in.

A machine earns the right to decide the way a person does: it makes a claim, answers for it, and bears the consequence of being wrong.

Observe · Predict · Commit · Learn

Consequence is the training signal. That machine does not exist yet. We are building it.

The machine that gets to decide should be the one that has to answer for it.

Join us

We are the researchers, developers, and builders behind leading ML tools and platforms. The researchers we work with have tens of thousands of citations.

We are hiring in research, graphs, time series, ML engineering, and product. If you are world‑class at one of those and want to build the thing that has to be right, write to us.

Write to us

join@ptl.inc

Done. Three desktop shots delivered — the mobile full-page failed to upload (1.0 MiB, server returned 400), so it's on disk at `restyle/shots/FINAL-mobile.png` if you want it.

## What shipped

**Branch `restyle/ptl-design-language`, commit `4b6efa2`.** Not pushed.

The page is a one-page argument in the design language your products actually share. The research found PTL has a real cross-app system — `ptl-trade`'s `globals.css` literally self-describes as *"matching ptl-console design language"* — so the landing page didn't need a new look invented, it needed the existing one applied: paper `#FAF8F5`, ink `#1E1E1E`, zero radius, 1px hairlines, no shadows, Cormorant for the argument and Geist Mono for machine chrome.

**The four beats, 315 words** (live page is 212 and has no approach beat at all): machines will make the decisions that matter → a language model is a memory → *"Confidence is easy. Accountability is the part nobody builds."* → a machine earns the right the way a person does. Closing line: *"The machine that gets to decide should be the one that has to answer for it."* Where the mechanism would go, the page stops.

**The scroll** moves exactly one attribute; CSS interpolates the rest. Nothing animates but opacity, geometry never changes — that's PTL's own house rule, and it makes reduced-motion and no-JS ship the fully-lit image rather than a degraded one. Both verified.

## Things I found and fixed that you didn't ask about

- **`--font-mono` was aliased to Cormorant**, so there was no mono face at all.
- **`html { font-size: 85% }` with a comment claiming 80**, and the wordmark's second line had been dead since `lg:text-5xl` lost to an unlayered shim rule — that's why "Text Labs." renders at 25.5px instead of 48px on the live site. All shim rules now sit in `@layer base`.
- **The footer's white `::before` scrim painted over content at `z-index: 9999`**, washing the recruiting sentence to near-illegibility at 1440×900 with no scrolling. Replaced with an opaque band.
- **Deploy surface**: 990 tracked files → 23.

## Two things need you

1. **`join@ptl.inc` is a proposal, not a verified address.** On a page whose thesis is accountability, a bouncing `mailto:` is the one bug that would actually be fatal. Confirm it or give me the real one.
2. **Mobile is 4.0 viewports** against the 2–3 ceiling; desktop is 2.86. I chose not to compress it further because the levers available (collapsing advisor entries, 15px bios) trade reading rhythm for a number. Say the word and I'll spend them.

On scroll-world: I used the mechanic, not the pipeline — the camera moves through the argument by illumination rather than translation. The scroll→camera mapping is isolated in one function, so if you authenticate Higgsfield later, a video painter drops in behind that seam without touching anything else.

One judgment worth flagging: I banned "balance sheet" from the copy. It's the memo's best line, but with finance framing around it, it's a two-second hop to "they trade." The bolder phrasings the workflow generated and declined are written up in `restyle/research/copy-strategy.md` for you to approve or reject rather than silently lose.

You're right on both counts, and the second one is the important one: **it doesn't do scroll storytelling at all.** Scroll-world's premise is a camera that genuinely moves through a world and pulls you forward. I reduced that to six faint marks changing opacity in the margins — the scroll does nothing narrative. That's not a weak version of the brief, it's a different thing.

Scrapping it. The existing attempt is committed on its branch, so nothing's lost, and I'm starting from pixels this time instead of from a document.

One change to how I run this: last round produced a rigorous *spec* that nobody looked at until I built it. This time every agent has to build a working prototype, screenshot its own output at multiple scroll positions, **look at the screenshots**, and iterate until it actually looks good before returning. And you'll judge them by scrolling them, not from stills — you can't evaluate motion from a still frame.

export const meta = {
  name: 'ptl-scroll-prototypes',
  description: 'Build four genuinely different, working scroll-storytelling prototypes for ptl.inc and iterate each until it looks good',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Prototype', detail: 'build, screenshot, critique own pixels, iterate' },
    { title: 'Critique', detail: 'independent visual judge per prototype' },
  ],
}

const W = '/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-janewang-Documents-GitHub-PTL-Landing/81f94152-0bf9-4cd6-a643-f5d5317526ce/scratchpad/restyle'
const P = `${W}/proto`

const COMMON = `
You are designing ptl.inc for Predictive Text Labs. A previous attempt was REJECTED by the client with
two words that matter: "ugly", and "it doesn't do the scroll storytelling". Read both criticisms as true.

=== WHAT WENT WRONG LAST TIME — do not repeat any of it ===
The last attempt was a static one-column document on light paper, with 34 small scattered squares as a
background "field" and six marginal 3-mark chains whose opacity changed as you scrolled. It failed because:
- The scattered marks read as dust, confetti or a rendering artifact. Not texture. Cheap.
- The lit chain read as a stray wireframe bracket, not an intentional graphic.
- The argument column was 544px inside a 1440px viewport with a permanently empty second column, so the
  page looked stranded and sparse rather than confident.
- Above all: SCROLL DID ALMOST NOTHING. Six opacity steps on marginal decoration is not storytelling.
  The reader scrolls and nothing travels, nothing transforms, nothing arrives.

=== THE ACTUAL BRIEF ===
Read ${W}/BRIEF.md IN FULL. It is binding, especially:
- §2b: the copy is the spine, four beats — (1) machines will make the decisions that matter;
  (2) models summarise the written past, they do not forecast; (3) accuracy alone cannot produce
  judgment, because nothing in a benchmark makes a machine answerable — only consequence does;
  (4) how we do it, withheld. Closing feeling: "they're right, and I want to know how."
- §3: DISCLOSURE RULES, non-negotiable. No performance figures, no trading, no venues, no product, no
  numbers in metric slots, no market iconography (candlesticks, order books, equity curves, up-and-to-
  the-right lines, dollar glyphs), no diverging red/green ramp. Sharp on the problem, vague ONLY on
  implementation.
- The page must remain a ONE-PAGER in spirit: one continuous idea, not a chaptered epic. Concision is a
  requirement — the whole argument should sit near 250-320 words.

Design-language research (palette, type, geometry, motion, voice) is in ${W}/design/DESIGN-LANGUAGE.md
and ${W}/research/*.md. PTL's own surfaces: warm paper #FAF8F5 / ink #1E1E1E in light, near-black
rgb(20,20,20) with cards at rgb(30,30,30) in dark, zero border radius, 1px hairlines, no shadows, warm
cream accent rgb(255,235,180) used almost never, Cormorant serif italic as the house signature, mono for
machine chrome, tabular figures. You may depart from any of this if your direction is better for it —
but say so and justify it.

=== SCROLL STORYTELLING IS THE POINT ===
Scroll must DRIVE A CAMERA OR A TRANSFORMATION that carries the argument. The reader should scroll
because they want the next thing, and something should genuinely travel, deepen, resolve or arrive.
Continuous — no hard cuts, no "sections fading in" (that is the generic AI-startup tell). The visual and
the sentence must be ONE object, not decoration beside prose.
Non-negotiable technical constraints: self-contained HTML, no external network requests, no frameworks,
no libraries. Canvas/SVG/CSS transforms are all fine. Must honour prefers-reduced-motion with a legible
static state. Must not jank — target 60fps, do work in rAF, never layout-thrash per frame.

=== HOW TO WORK — THIS IS THE PART THAT CHANGED ===
You will BUILD, LOOK, AND ITERATE. You are not writing a design document. Nobody wants a document.

1. Create your directory: ${P}/<ID>/  and write index.html there (self-contained).
   Fonts: run  ln -s /Users/janewang/Documents/GitHub/PTL-Landing/fonts ${P}/<ID>/fonts
   so /fonts/Cormorant%20Variable%20Font.woff2, /fonts/Cormorant%20Italic%20Variable%20Font.woff2 and
   /fonts/GeistMono.woff2 resolve. Geist Mono is a variable woff2, weights 100-900.
2. Serve it on YOUR OWN PORT (given below), in the background:
   cd ${P}/<ID> && python3 -m http.server <PORT> --bind 127.0.0.1
3. Screenshot it at MANY scroll positions with Playwright:
   const {chromium} = require('/Users/janewang/Documents/GitHub/ptl-console/node_modules/.pnpm/playwright@1.58.2/node_modules/playwright')
   Use browser.newPage({viewport:{width:1440,height:900}, deviceScaleFactor:2}).
   NOTE: the option is \`viewport\`, NOT \`viewportSize\` — getting this wrong silently renders every shot
   at the default size and you will draw false conclusions.
   Capture at least 8 evenly-spaced scroll positions, plus 390x844 mobile.
4. **READ YOUR OWN SCREENSHOTS with the Read tool and judge them honestly.** This is the step that was
   missing last time. Ask: is this beautiful? Would a designer I respect ship this? Does the scroll
   actually carry a story, or is it decoration? Is anything reading as debris, clipart, or a default?
5. ITERATE. Minimum THREE build-look-fix rounds. Do not return after one. Most first attempts are ugly;
   the work is in the revision. If a device isn't working, delete it rather than tuning it.
6. Only return when you would defend it to a hostile art director.

Write a short README.md in your directory: the idea in three sentences, what scroll does, what you tried
and rejected, and your honest assessment of its weakest point. Keep it SHORT — the prototype is the
deliverable, not the prose.
`

const SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  additionalProperties: false,
  required: ['id', 'name', 'port', 'idea', 'whatScrollDoes', 'rounds', 'weakest', 'selfScore'],
  properties: {
    id: { type: 'string' },
    name: { type: 'string' },
    port: { type: 'number' },
    idea: { type: 'string', description: 'the direction in 2-3 sentences' },
    whatScrollDoes: { type: 'string', description: 'precisely what scroll drives' },
    rounds: { type: 'number', description: 'how many build-look-fix rounds you actually completed' },
    weakest: { type: 'string', description: 'the honest weakest point' },
    selfScore: { type: 'number', description: '0-100, how good you actually think it looks' },
  },
}

const DIRS = [
  {
    id: 'A', port: 5401, label: 'proto:dive',
    stance: `THE DIVE. A dark, deep, continuous camera flight. Scroll flies the camera FORWARD through
layered depth — the reader is travelling into something, and the beats arrive as they pass through. This
is the closest to scroll-world's original conceit (a camera that genuinely moves, no cuts), rendered in
code rather than video: CSS 3D transforms or canvas, parallax layers at true different depths, things
passing the camera. It should feel cinematic and a little vertiginous. The danger to beat: cheap
starfield / "space" clichés, and parallax that reads as a template. Make the depth mean something —
the reader is going somewhere, and arriving.`,
  },
  {
    id: 'B', port: 5402, label: 'proto:resolve',
    stance: `THE RESOLUTION. The page opens in noise and resolves. Scroll drives a transformation from
dense uncertainty into structure — thousands of fine particles, grains or probability density that
coalesce, sharpen and settle as the argument advances, and at the end become one clean form. The subject
is uncertainty becoming judgment, which is exactly the argument, so the visual IS the thesis rather than
an illustration of it. Canvas, thousands of elements, real per-frame work done efficiently. The danger to
beat: generic particle-demo aesthetics, and anything that reads as a data chart. It must never resolve
into a graph, a curve, or an arrow.`,
  },
  {
    id: 'C', port: 5403, label: 'proto:type',
    stance: `TYPOGRAPHIC CINEMA. No illustration whatsoever. The TYPE is the cinematography. Words at
enormous scale, occupying the full viewport, choreographed by scroll — scale, weight, opacity, position,
masking, one line handing to the next. Think a great editorial title sequence, not a website. Every beat
gets its own frame of the film. This should feel expensive and confident and completely unlike an AI
startup page. You have Cormorant (300-700, roman + italic) and Geist Mono. The danger to beat: it
becoming a slideshow of fading paragraphs, which is the generic tell. It must feel continuous and
composed, with real typographic craft — kerning, scale relationships, tension between the serif and the
mono.`,
  },
  {
    id: 'D', port: 5404, label: 'proto:branch',
    stance: `BRANCHING FUTURES. The page is one continuous structure that starts as a single line and
opens into many possible paths, and scroll travels along it. Many futures exist; most stay unresolved;
the camera moves through the branching. This is genuinely on-theme (forecasting is reasoning about which
future arrives) and it is native to how PTL draws. But it must NOT look like a flowchart, an org chart, a
decision tree diagram, or a network graph — and it must never read as a chart with axes or an
up-and-to-the-right line. Consider drawing it very large, so the reader is INSIDE the structure rather
than looking at a diagram of it. Dark or light, your call.`,
  },
]

phase('Prototype')
log('Four working prototypes. Each agent builds, screenshots, reads its own pixels, and iterates at least three rounds.')

const built = await pipeline(
  DIRS,
  (d) =>
    agent(
      `${COMMON}

YOUR DIRECTION — ${d.id}. YOUR PORT — ${d.port}. YOUR DIRECTORY — ${P}/${d.id}/

${d.stance}

Build it. Look at it. Fix it. At least three rounds. Return the structured summary.`,
      { label: d.label, phase: 'Prototype', schema: SCHEMA, effort: 'max' }
    ),
  (proto, d) => {
    if (!proto) return null
    return agent(
      `You are a hostile art director reviewing a landing-page prototype for Predictive Text Labs.

The prototype is at ${P}/${d.id}/index.html. Its own screenshots are in ${P}/${d.id}/ (look for .png
files). Serve it yourself if you need fresh captures:
  cd ${P}/${d.id} && python3 -m http.server ${d.port + 100} --bind 127.0.0.1
and screenshot with Playwright from
/Users/janewang/Documents/GitHub/ptl-console/node_modules/.pnpm/playwright@1.58.2/node_modules/playwright
(use browser.newPage({viewport:{width:1440,height:900}, deviceScaleFactor:2}) — the option is
\`viewport\`, not \`viewportSize\`). Capture at least 8 scroll positions and LOOK at every one with the
Read tool. Judge pixels, not intentions.

The brief is ${W}/BRIEF.md. The previous attempt was rejected as "ugly" and for not doing scroll
storytelling, so you are calibrated to be harsh about exactly those two things.

Score these, each out of 20, and be a hard marker — most work is 55-70 and above 85 means you would
personally ship it:
1. Is it actually beautiful? Would a designer you respect ship it? Name what is cheap or default.
2. Does scroll genuinely tell the story — does something travel, deepen, resolve or arrive — or is it
   decoration beside prose?
3. Craft: typography, composition, colour, restraint, motion quality. Is anything janky, jittery, or
   reading as debris/clipart/template?
4. Does the argument land, and does the page stay disclosure-safe (BRIEF §3)?
5. Would it survive on a phone and under prefers-reduced-motion?

Return your verdict. Name the single strongest idea in it and the single thing that would most improve
it. Do not be agreeable.`,
      { label: `judge:${d.id}`, phase: 'Critique', effort: 'max' }
    ).then((v) => ({ proto, verdict: v, dir: d }))
  }
)

const ok = built.filter((b) => b && b.proto && b.verdict)
const lost = DIRS.filter((d, i) => !built[i] || !built[i].proto || !built[i].verdict).map((d) => d.label)

if (lost.length) {
  log(`INCOMPLETE — ${lost.join(', ')} did not finish. Prototypes on disk are intact.`)
  return { status: 'PARTIAL', missing: lost, delivered: ok.map((b) => ({ id: b.dir.id, port: b.dir.port, proto: b.proto, verdict: b.verdict })) }
}

return {
  status: 'OK',
  prototypes: ok.map((b) => ({ id: b.dir.id, name: b.proto.name, port: b.dir.port, dir: `${P}/${b.dir.id}`, proto: b.proto, verdict: b.verdict })),
}

That's the real problem, and it's more damning than "ugly." Look at what the actual PTL apps are:

**PTL Trade** — near-black ground, panels one step up, **one saturated hue per category** carried on the card border *and* its big tabular numeral, uppercase mono micro-labels, status pills (`ARMED` / `WATCH` / `LIVE`), orthogonal routed connectors with filleted corners, **dim-vs-lit opacity as the information channel**, italic serif wordmark as the one humanist note.

**PTL Chat** — same near-black, italic serif page titles, micro-label-over-big-numeral stat strips, left accent bars for grouping, tiny pills, and white roman prose immediately qualified by *grey italic serif*.

**Backtesting** — same ground, inverted white pill for the active tab, left accent rule for the gate callout, label→value rows.

There's a real, distinctive, good-looking house language across all three. I built a **cream serif letterpress page** — the exact opposite of it. Two of the four in-flight prototypes even inherited that same cream palette, so they'd have landed in the same hole.

28	**The strength of this page is the copy.** Not the visual, not the chrome, not the scroll mechanic. The
29	argument carries the page; everything else exists to make someone keep reading it. If a design decision
30	and a sentence compete, the sentence wins.
31	
32	### The arc — four beats, in this order
33	
34	1. **This is the future.** Machines will make the consequential decisions — in finance, in business, in
35	   government. State it as a fact about the world, not as a prediction about us. The reader should feel
36	   the inevitability before they feel any pitch.
37	2. **This is how the future gets closer.** Not "here is our product" — the *condition* that has to be
38	   met for that future to arrive at all. Today's models summarise the written past; they do not forecast.
39	   The future is waiting on something that does not exist yet.
40	3. **This is the only way to solve it.** The heart. Accuracy alone cannot get there, because nothing in a
41	   benchmark makes a machine answerable — a confident error vanishes inside a good average, and software
42	   charges the same fee whether it was right or wrong. The only thing that produces judgment is
43	   **consequence**: a machine that commits something scarce, is answerable for being wrong, and improves
44	   when reality resolves. Make this feel like a discovered necessity, not a claim.
45	4. **How we do it — withheld.** The mechanism is where the page goes quiet. Not evasive, not coy:
46	   *deliberate*. The reader should finish convinced the problem is real, convinced there is only one way
47	   through it, and genuinely unable to say what PTL builds.
48	
49	The reader's closing thought should be **"they're right, and I want to know how"** — never
50	*"what do they actually do?"* as a complaint. Curiosity, not confusion.
51	
52	### Vagueness is directional, not uniform
53	
54	Be sharp and concrete about the **problem** and about **why consequence is the only answer**. Be vague
55	only about **implementation** — what we build, what it runs on, what it touches, what it produces.
56	A reader should be able to argue the thesis back to a colleague and still not know the company's business.
57	
58	### Concision is a hard requirement
59	
60	**As short as it can be while still landing.** This is the discipline that makes the argument feel
61	inevitable rather than pleaded. Prefer a sentence to a paragraph, and a clause to a sentence. Cut every
62	line that merely restates a previous one — the current page has several. If a beat can be carried in six
63	words, it does not get twenty. Ruthlessness here is the difference between austere and windy.
64	
65	### What the scroll is for
66	
67	The scroll exists to **keep someone reading** — it is a pacing device for an argument, not a ride.
68	Each beat should earn the next scroll: the reader moves because they want the next line, not because
69	there is more page. Reveal on scroll should feel like the argument advancing. Never let the visual
70	outshine, delay, or talk over the sentence it accompanies; if a reader remembers the animation and not
71	the argument, the page has failed.
72	
73	## 3. Disclosure Rules — NON-NEGOTIABLE
74	
75	### 3a. FORBIDDEN — must never appear, in any form, including implication, iconography, chart shapes, or clever paraphrase
76	
77	- **Any performance number whatsoever**: the ~50% time-weighted return, Brier scores (0.121 / 0.129), Sharpe ratio, instrument counts, trade counts, win rates, month-over-month figures, backtest results.
78	- **The fact that we trade markets.** No trading, positions, P&L, portfolio, book, execution, fills, spreads, capital allocation, sizing, hedge fund, prop desk, returns.
79	- **Named venues or instruments**: Polymarket, Kalshi, prediction markets, options, commodity futures, TradFi, equities, tickers.
80	- **What the product actually is.** No product name, no API, no dashboard, no "we sell forecasts", no customer-facing offering, no pricing, no consulting-market sizing.
81	- **Fundraise material**: the $700K SAFE, the $1.3M round, valuation, runway, burn, cash position, investor language, "bridge".
82	- **Team/employer specifics used as proof of the above**: do not name Point72, Susquehanna, or the Allen Institute in a way that signals a trading operation.
83	- Do not put any of the above in HTML comments, `alt` text, meta tags, structured data, filenames, or CSS class names. Assume everything ships is readable.
84	
85	### 3b. ALLOWED — the raw material for problem + approach
86	
87	- Machines will make most consequential decisions in finance, business and government within ~20 years; the open question is *which* machine earns the right to decide.
88	- LLMs are trained on the written past. They summarise it brilliantly. They are not built to forecast — their probabilities largely echo what is already written or already priced.
89	- Reasoning to predict events is fundamentally different from predicting the next token. Real forecasting means seeing how events cascade, why patterns repeat, and which signals matter.
90	- Temporal reasoning is not one more capability — it is the primitive that turns a model from a search engine into a decision-making partner.
91	- **Accountability is the missing ingredient, and this is the heart of the approach:**
92	  - A benchmark cannot create it — a dangerously confident error disappears inside a strong average.
93	  - Software cannot create it — the fee is the same whether an individual prediction was right or wrong.
94	  - Therefore a machine earns the right to decide only by **committing something scarce, bearing the consequence of being wrong, and improving when reality resolves.**
95	- The loop, stated abstractly: **observe → predict → commit → act → resolve → learn.** Consequence is the training signal.
96	- Where the world proves the machine right, it advances; where it proves the machine wrong, it learns. (Abstract phrasing only — do not render this as profit/loss.)
97	- Recruiting: researchers, developers and builders behind leading ML tools and platforms; the researchers we work with have tens of thousands of citations; hiring in research, graphs, time series, ML engineering, product.
98	- Founders and advisors exactly as currently listed on the page.
99	
100	### 3b-bis. The screenshots in `shots/` are CONTAMINATED — look at form, never content
101	
102	The reference screenshots were captured from live internal tools. Several contain material that is
103	squarely forbidden by 3a: strategy names, instrument identifiers, position values, monetary amounts,
104	run outcomes, and real forecast subject matter. `trade-dashboard-light.png` alone shows a metric strip
105	with a position count and a dollar figure, plus named strategies and instrument targets.
106	
107	**You are looking at these images for FORM ONLY**: colour, type, spacing, geometry, density, hairlines,
108	motion, chrome. Treat every string, number, glyph and label inside them as radioactive. Do not quote it,
109	do not adapt it, do not "genericise" it into a similar-looking placeholder, and do not reproduce a
110	component *because of* what it displays. Copying the metric-strip **pattern** (uppercase micro-label +
111	value on a hairline rule) is fine and encouraged; copying anything that reads as a performance figure
112	is a hard fail — including invented numbers that merely occupy the same slot. If the landing page shows
113	a number in a metric-strip slot, a reader will read it as performance. **So the page ships no metrics.**
114	
115	### 3c. The line, stated once more
116	
117	**The *shape* of the approach is sayable. The *instrument* is not.**
118	
119	"A machine that pays for being wrong" — allowed.
120	"A machine with a balance sheet" — **too close, do not use.** "Balance sheet", "capital", "stake", "wager", "bet", "position" all read as trading to the target audience. Use consequence/commitment/accountability language instead.
121	
122	If you are unsure whether a phrase crosses the line, it crosses the line. Write the safer version and note the bolder alternative separately in your report so a human can decide.
123	
124	## 4. Design direction
125	
126	- Must read as a sibling of PTL's internal product surfaces (`ptl-trade` web, `ptl-chat-py` app, `ptl-backtesting` dashboard). Research findings for these live in `research/`.
127	- The current page's restraint is an asset, not a deficiency: Cormorant serif, `stone-100` ground, enormous whitespace, near-zero chrome, no navigation, no buttons, no logos.
128	- **Scroll-world mechanic, code-rendered.** Scroll should drive a continuous camera through a single coherent visual — implemented in canvas/WebGL/SVG/CSS, NOT AI-generated video. No `higgsfield`/`monid`/`ffmpeg` in this build. The visual must never illustrate a forbidden concept (no candlesticks, order books, equity curves, up-and-to-the-right lines, dollar signs, market charts).
129	  - *Future-proofing, at zero cost now:* this is pass one. If it lands, a later pass may add AI-rendered video through the scroll-world pipeline. So keep the scroll→camera mapping in one small, isolated module with a clean seam between "what drives the camera" and "what gets painted". Do **not** compromise this pass's design to accommodate that — just don't weld the two together.
130	- Ship-shape constraint: the repo is static HTML + Tailwind v4 built via `npm run build:css`, `outputDirectory: "."` on Vercel. Whatever is designed must ship inside that, with no framework migration.
131	- Accessibility and performance are part of "best": honour `prefers-reduced-motion`, keep the page fast, keep text real text.
132	
133	## 5. Deliverable discipline
134	
135	Every agent writes its findings to a file under the workspace **before** returning, so work survives an interruption. Return a short structured result, not a wall of prose.
136

The ptl.inc landing restyle must derive its visual language from PTL's internal
product surfaces, which are **dark instruments**, not from the legacy light page.
A cream/`#FAF8F5` Cormorant editorial treatment was built and rejected twice —
"truly ugly" and "doesnt take the design at all from the reference repos".

**Why:** the brief's own §4 wrongly framed the existing page's cream restraint as
"an asset", so the first build preserved a palette that is the visual opposite of
every real PTL surface. The goal is for the page to read as a sibling of the
products, so the products' language wins over the incumbent page's.

**How to apply:** the house system, sampled from the apps' own pixels —
ground `#141414`, panel `#1e1e1e`, hairline `#3c3c3c`, primary text `#f0f0f0`,
secondary `#a0a0a0`, tertiary `#818181`, cream accent `#ffebb4`; radius 0.
Taxonomy colour is a strict triad per hue — dark saturated border, near-black
tinted fill, bright saturated ink: amber `#bb4d00`/`#22140e`/`#f08610`,
green `#008236`/`#0e1b14`/`#00c950`, blue `#1447e6`/`#141d2a`/`#2b7fff`
(Tailwind v4 hues on custom neutrals). Signature moves: italic serif wordmark and
page titles as the one humanist note, uppercase mono micro-labels, tiny status
pills, left accent rules, dim-vs-lit opacity used as an information channel, and
`—` as the glyph for "nothing exists to report".

Reference screenshots are contaminated with forbidden content — study form only,
never strings or numbers. See [[ptl-landing-disclosure-line]]. CSS and HTML
comments ship, so they must not name the internal apps either.

Three options are live. One server, three URLs — scroll them, the whole point is in the motion:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **1 · The Chain** | http://127.0.0.1:5410/chain.html | 3.7 vh |
| **2 · The Field** | http://127.0.0.1:5410/field.html | 3.9 vh |

**What changed at the root.** I sampled the actual pixels of your three apps instead of trusting the research reports. They share one system: ground `#141414`, panel `#1e1e1e`, hairline `#3c3c3c`, text `#f0f0f0`/`#a0a0a0`/`#818181` — Tailwind v4 hues on custom near-blacks. Taxonomy colour is always a triad: dark saturated border, near-black tinted fill, bright saturated ink (`#bb4d00`/`#22140e`/`#f08610`). Plus the italic serif wordmark as the one humanist note, mono micro-labels, status pills, and dim-vs-lit opacity used as *information*. All three options are built on that, shared in one `ptl.css`.

**The scroll device is the same in all three, and it's an argument, not decoration.** The loop strip along the foot runs `OBSERVE → PREDICT → COMMIT → LEARN`. It lights as you read — and then **deliberately stalls** at "The missing test," where the right-hand readout reads `LOOP INCOMPLETE`. It only closes at "Earning the right." The chrome makes your point before the prose does. The chain then terminates in a dashed, empty `HOW` node holding a single `—`, the glyph beat 1 taught you to read.

They differ in how the page carries weight: **1** uses hued panels on a lighting spine (most like the thesis map, handsomest); **2** replaces boxes with a full-bleed embedding that starts as undifferentiated noise and resolves into four hued clusters (fills the margins, and the visual *is* "past → structure"); **3** drops boxes entirely for full-bleed hairlines that sweep across the viewport in the beat's hue (most typographically confident, most austere).

**My pick is 1**, with the margin problem fixed by borrowing 2's field at much lower density — 3's type is the best of the three but it's the longest and the widest column.

Honest gaps: all three run longer than the 2–3 viewport target I'd set (the argument itself is ~340 words; the roster is the tail); `join@ptl.inc` is still an unverified address and a bouncing mailto would be the one fatal bug here; and nothing is committed — the rejected build is parked on `restyle/ptl-design-language`, `main` is untouched.

One thing worth flagging: my own CSS comments were naming the internal apps and quoting a strip label from one of their UIs, and `ptl.css` ships. Scrubbed, and the files now pass a clean leak scan — but it's a reminder that comments are shipped text.

content.text:
**Cormorant** — the Christian Thalmann / Catharsis Fonts display serif (SIL Open Font License), version 4.000.

It's self-hosted as two variable woff2 files in `fonts/`, both carrying a `wght` axis from **300 to 700**:

| file | style |
|---|---|
| `Cormorant Variable Font.woff2` | roman |
| `Cormorant Italic Variable Font.woff2` | italic |

Both are declared under the family name `"Cormorant"` in `index.html:90–103`, with `font-display: swap` and a `ui-serif, Georgia, serif` fallback stack. The prototypes use the exact same two files via a symlink, so nothing diverged.

Two details worth knowing since you're editing:

The **default weight is 300**, not 400 — the axis starts there. So anything that doesn't set a weight renders Light, and `font-weight: 400` is a real step up rather than the neutral position.

And the files' internal family name is `Cormorant Light`, which is just how the variable build was named upstream; the `@font-face` rule overrides it, so `"Cormorant"` is the correct name to use in CSS. It's plain Cormorant, not Cormorant Garamond or Cormorant Infant — those are separate families with different letterforms.

The mono alongside it is **Geist Mono**, subset to 22.8 KB, used for the micro-labels, pills, and `ptl.inc`.
